clinical_knowledge.topic: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Immediately discontinue offending medications (minocycline and oral contraceptive pill), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: daily throbbing headache and whooshing sound in ears for 2 months

Key HPI features: 2-month history of daily, severe, generalized throbbing headaches that are worse in the morning on waking and exacerbated by coughing, straining, or bending forward. Experiences a rhythmic whooshing noise in both ears synchronised with her heartbeat (pulsatile tinnitus). Reports transient 5-second episodes of complete visual darkening or grey-out (transient visual obscurations) triggered whenever she stands up quickly or bends over to tie her shoes. Gained 15kg over the past year.

Objective/Exam findings: Fundoscopy: bilateral grade IV papilloedema (blurred disc margins, loss of venous pulsations, peripapillary flame haemorrhages). Visual field testing: enlarged blind spots and early nasal step/peripheral constriction. Cranial nerve exam: check for bilateral VIth nerve palsy (false localizing sign of raised ICP causing horizontal diplopia). Urgent MRI Brain with MR Venography (normal brain parenchyma without mass/hydrocephalus; MRV rules out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and shows transverse sinus stenosis/empty sella). Lumbar puncture in lateral decubitus position: opening pressure markedly elevated (>25 cm H2O, often >30-40 cm H2O) with completely normal CSF constituents.
Relevant background/PMH: obesity (BMI 36), polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), mild acne
Current medications: combined oral contraceptive pill, minocycline 100mg OD for acne over past 4 months
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any visual field loss or progression — optic nerve damage can become permanent.
management_principles: Immediately discontinue offending medications (minocycline and oral contraceptive pill)
Initiate carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide starting 500mg BID up-titrated up to 2g daily) to decrease CSF production
Urgent ophthalmology referral for regular visual field monitoring (critical instructions: permanent optic atrophy and blindness can occur if uncontrolled)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 26F with recent weight gain and minocycline/OCP exposure presents with signs of raised intracranial pressure: morning throbbing headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations on posture change.
reference_soap.objective: Fundoscopy: bilateral grade IV papilloedema (blurred disc margins, loss of venous pulsations, peripapillary flame haemorrhages). Visual field testing: enlarged blind spots and early nasal step/peripheral constriction. Cranial nerve exam: check for bilateral VIth nerve palsy (false localizing sign of raised ICP causing horizontal diplopia). Urgent MRI Brain with MR Venography (normal brain parenchyma without mass/hydrocephalus; MRV rules out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and shows transverse sinus stenosis/empty sella). Lumbar puncture in lateral decubitus position: opening pressure markedly elevated (>25 cm H2O, often >30-40 cm H2O) with completely normal CSF constituents.
reference_soap.assessment: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri) likely exacerbated by minocycline and rapid weight gain. DDx: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST), intracranial mass lesion, obstructive hydrocephalus, secondary intracranial hypertension from tetracyclines/retinoids.
reference_soap.plan: Immediately discontinue offending medications (minocycline and oral contraceptive pill). Initiate carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide starting 500mg BID up-titrated up to 2g daily) to decrease CSF production. Urgent ophthalmology referral for regular visual field monitoring (critical instructions: permanent optic atrophy and blindness can occur if uncontrolled). Structured multidisciplinary weight loss management (target 10-15% body weight reduction is curative in many cases). Neurosurgical referral for optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting if visual fields deteriorate despite medical therapy.

learning_objectives: Identify the classical symptom triad of raised intracranial pressure: morning headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations
Correlate epidemiological risk factors (young obese female) and drug exposures (tetracyclines, retinoids, contraceptives) with IIH pathogenesis
Explain the mandatory sequence of neuroimaging (MRI/MRV to exclude mass or venous sinus thrombosis) prior to diagnostic lumbar puncture
Emphasize the urgent priority of visual field monitoring to prevent irreversible optic atrophy

teaching.one_liner: Elevated pressure around the brain without a mass — typically in young obese women — causing daily morning headaches worse with straining, pulsatile tinnitus, and brief 'graying out' of vision on standing; untreated, it can cause permanent blindness.
red_flags: Any visual field loss or progression — optic nerve damage can become permanent

must_ask.say: Is the headache worse in the morning, and does it get worse when you cough or bend over?
Do you hear a whooshing sound in your ears that matches your heartbeat?
Do you have brief moments where your vision goes gray or dark, especially when standing up?
How much weight have you gained recently?
Are you taking any acne medications like minocycline, or birth control pills?
